title: A Study of Shakespeare
description: Published in 1880 and the most brilliant critical book of the Victorian age: a study of Shakespeare's development through the metre of his plays.
plot_or_argument: Swinburne traces the verse of the plays from the early histories to The Tempest, and reads the metrical development as the index of the poet's growth, in three chapters ('First Period', 'Second Period', 'Third Period') of extraordinary literary prose.
historical_context: 1870s: the Victorian Shakespeare industry, the new metrical criticism, and the 'disintegration' controversy over the authorship of the plays.
literary_significance: A Study of Shakespeare is the central Victorian critical study of the dramatist and one of the seminal works of English metrical criticism: its method and its prose shaped the modern reading of Shakespeare's development.

title: Poems and Ballads, Second Series
description: Published in 1878 and the second and more mature collection of Swinburne's lyrics: the poems of the sea, of death and of the classical world.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'A Forsaken Garden', 'The Last Oracle', 'Ave Atque Vale' (the elegy for Baudelaire), 'Relics', 'At Parting' and the sonnets on the death of his sister, and is the finest of Swinburne's later collections.
historical_context: 1870s: the death of Baudelaire and the English Decadence, and Swinburne's withdrawal from London.
literary_significance: Poems and Ballads, Second Series contains some of the greatest English lyrics of the century, including 'A Forsaken Garden' and the elegy for Baudelaire; it shows Swinburne at the height of his powers after the scandal of 1866.

title: The Earthly Paradise
description: Published in three volumes between 1868 and 1870 and the most popular long poem of the Victorian age after Idylls of the King: a frame narrative of wanderers in search of a deathless land, and the tales they tell.
plot_or_argument: A company of medieval Norsemen sail west in search of the Earthly Paradise and come instead to an island of Greek descendants, where the two groups exchange stories month by month through the year; the twenty-four tales include 'The Story of Cupid and Psyche', 'Atalanta's Race' and 'The Doom of King Acrisius'.
historical_context: 1860s: the Pre-Raphaelite movement, the Kelmscott circle, and the Victorian taste for the long narrative poem.
literary_significance: The Earthly Paradise is the central Pre-Raphaelite poem and one of the great narrative works of the century: its tales, its frame and its decorative design made it the model for the Victorian long poem and the direct ancestor of the modern fantasy tradition.

title: News from Nowhere; or, An Epoch of Rest
description: Serialised in the Socialist League's Commonweal in 1890 and Morris's most influential prose work: the dream of a socialist England of the twenty-first century.
plot_or_argument: William Guest falls asleep after a meeting of the Socialist League and wakes in a pastoral, decentralised England of the twenty-second century, where money and government have disappeared, work is a pleasure, and the Thames is clean; he travels up the river with Dick and Clara and old Hammond, and wakes back in the nineteenth century.
historical_context: 1890: the Socialist League, the arts and crafts movement, and the English socialist revival of the 1880s.
literary_significance: News from Nowhere is the classic English socialist utopia and one of the most influential utopian works in the language: its vision of a decentralised, craft-based, ecological society made it the founding text of the green and the anti-industrial utopia.

title: A Dream of John Ball
description: Serialised in the Commonweal in 1886-87 and published in 1888: a time-travel fantasy of the Peasants' Revolt, in which the narrator joins the rebels of 1381.
plot_or_argument: William Langland's dreamer is transported to the village of Bletchingley in 1381, joins the peasants led by Wat Tyler and John Ball, hears Ball's sermon on the equality of men, and returns to the nineteenth century with a vision of the long struggle for freedom continuing to his own day.
historical_context: 1381: the Peasants' Revolt, the preaching of John Ball, the socialism of the 1880s, and the Victorian socialist revival of the medieval past.
literary_significance: A Dream of John Ball is the finest English historical fantasy of the century and a founding text of the socialist historical novel: its sermon on equality and its vision of the long revolution made it a central text of the English labour movement.

title: Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs
description: Published in 1876 and Morris's greatest poem: a retelling of the Norse Volsunga saga, the source of the Nibelungenlied and of Wagner's Ring.
plot_or_argument: Sigurd slays the dragon Fafnir, wins the hoard and the ring Andvaranaut, awakens Brynhild on Hindfell, is drugged and marries Gudrun, and is murdered by the Niblungs; the poem ends with Gudrun's revenge and the destruction of the Niblung house.
historical_context: 1876: the Victorian interest in the Norse sagas, the Icelandic scholarship of the period, and Wagner's Ring (first performed complete in 1876).
literary_significance: Sigurd the Volsung is the finest English epic poem of the nineteenth century and the central text of the Victorian Norse revival: its influence on Tolkien, on the modern fantasy and on the English idea of the heroic is enormous.

title: The Defence of Guenevere and Other Poems
description: Published in 1858 and Morris's first book: a collection of dramatic lyrics of the Arthurian and medieval world, which puzzled the reviewers and later became one of the founding texts of the Pre-Raphaelite movement.
plot_or_argument: The title poem is Guenevere's defence before her accusers; the volume also contains 'King Arthur's Tomb', 'The Haystack in the Floods', 'Concerning Geffray Teste Noire' and the dramatic lyrics of the French and English middle ages.
historical_context: 1850s: the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, the Oxford of Burne-Jones and Rossetti, and the Victorian medieval revival.
literary_significance: The Defence of Guenevere is the founding book of Pre-Raphaelite poetry and one of the great collections of dramatic lyrics in English: its treatment of Guenevere's desire and its grim realism about violence made it a permanent influence on the twentieth-century Arthurian tradition.

title: The Symbolist Movement in Literature
description: Published in 1899 and the most influential critical book of the English 1890s: the study that introduced French Symbolism to the English-speaking world.
plot_or_argument: Symons traces the Symbolist movement from Gérard de Nerval and Baudelaire through Verlaine, Rimbaud, Mallarmé, Laforgue and Huysmans, and argues that literature is the expression of an invisible world through the symbol rather than the description of the visible one.
historical_context: 1890s: the French Symbolist movement, the English Decadence, and the crisis of realism in the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Symbolist Movement in Literature is one of the most influential critical books ever published in English: it taught Yeats, Eliot, Pound and Joyce how to read modern French poetry and helped to create the poetics of literary modernism.

title: London Nights
description: Published in 1895 and the central collection of English Decadent city poetry: the poems of the music hall, the ballet, the prostitute's room and the London night.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'To the Recollection of the Music-Hall', 'Nora on the Pavement', 'The Absinthe Drinker', 'Ideala' and 'Gray Nights', in which the pleasures and exhaustions of the urban night are rendered with a quite modern frankness.
historical_context: 1890s: the London music hall and ballet, the Savoy and the Café Royal, and the English reception of the French Decadence.
literary_significance: London Nights is the founding book of English urban Decadence and one of the first English collections to make the music hall and the streetwalker the subjects of serious lyric: its poetry of the city night made possible the urban poetry of the twentieth century.

title: Days and Nights
description: Published in 1889 and Symons's first collection of verse: the poems of the aesthete's sensations, the theatre, the sea and the passing of pleasure.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'A Prelude', 'At Dieppe', 'The Opium Smoker', 'Nerves', 'On the Beach' and the poems of love and weariness that established the tone of the English Decadent lyric.
historical_context: 1889: the Rhymers' Club, the English reception of Pater, and the aesthetic culture of the late 1880s.
literary_significance: Days and Nights founded the English Decadent lyric of the 1890s and established the tone that Dowson, Johnson and the Rhymers' Club would develop.

title: The Savoy
description: Edited by Symons with Aubrey Beardsley in 1896 and the central magazine of the English Decadence: eight numbers that printed the work of Yeats, Dowson, Johnson, Beardsley, Conrad and Shaw.
plot_or_argument: The Savoy published poetry, fiction, criticism and drawings of the Decadent school, defended itself against the charge of obscenity, and printed the first instalment of Conrad's The Nigger of the 'Narcissus'.
historical_context: 1896: the Wilde trials and the collapse of the Decadent market, and the new little magazine culture.
literary_significance: The Savoy is the central magazine of the English Decadence and one of the most important little magazines in English literary history: its eight numbers preserve the work of a whole movement and its collapse marks the end of the 1890s aesthetic moment.

title: 'Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae'
description: Published in the Second Book of the Rhymers' Club in 1894 and the most famous English Decadent lyric: the poem of the lover who has betrayed his beloved and cannot forget her.
plot_or_argument: The speaker recounts the nights of wine and roses and the women he has held, and after each stanza returns to the refrain 'I am desolate and sick of an old passion, / Yea, hungry for the lips of my desire: / I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion.'
literary_form: Lyric poem (in The Second Book of the Rhymers' Club, 1894)
meter_and_prosody: Five five-line stanzas of iambic metre, with the Latin epigraph from Horace and the refrain drawn from Catullus.
historical_context: 1894: the Rhymers' Club, the London of the music hall and the restaurant, and the Latin poetry of Catullus and Propertius.
literary_significance: 'Non sum qualis eram' is the central English Decadent poem and one of the most quoted lyrics in the language: its refrain entered common speech, and its fusion of classical Latin and modern self-disgust made it the model for the modern poem of sexual betrayal.

title: Verses (1896)
description: Published in 1896 and Dowson's first collection: the lyrics of renunciation, wine and hopeless love that made him the most admired poet of his generation.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'Villanelle of Sunset', 'To One in Bedlam', 'The Three Witches', 'Spleen', 'Extreme Unction' and 'Vain Resolves', and its subject is the exhaustion of desire in the shadow of death.
historical_context: 1896: the English Decadence at its height, the Rhymers' Club, and Dowson's own poverty and illness.
literary_significance: Verses contains the purest body of English Decadent lyric poetry: its perfection of form and its absolute refusal of consolation made Dowson the poet's poet of the 1890s and an influence on Yeats and Eliot.

title: Dilemmas: Studies in Sentiment
description: Published in 1895 and Dowson's finest prose: a collection of stories of moral and emotional exhaustion, in the manner of Pater and Huysmans.
plot_or_argument: The stories include 'A Dilemma', 'The Diary of a Successful Man', 'An Orchestral Violin' and 'The Statute of Limitations', and each turns on a moment of recognition in which the protagonist sees the emptiness of his life.
historical_context: 1890s: the English Decadent prose tradition after Pater, and the aesthetic short story.
literary_significance: Dilemmas is the finest collection of English Decadent short stories and the prose counterpart to Dowson's verse: its study of emotional exhaustion made it a key text of the 1890s.

title: Decorations
description: Published in 1899 and Dowson's second collection: the poems written in the last years of his life, when he had renounced the world and returned to the Catholic faith of his childhood.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Dead Child', 'Benedictio Domini', 'A Last Word', 'Vesperal' and the poems of renunciation and prayer; its subject is the exhaustion of pleasure and the turning to God.
historical_context: 1899: the Catholic revival, Dowson's illness and poverty, and the end of the Decadent decade.
literary_significance: Decorations is the finest religious poetry of the English Decadence and the record of a deathbed conversion: it completes the arc from the paganism of Swinburne to the Catholicism of Thompson and Johnson, and it is one of the great small volumes of English verse.

title: Poems (1895)
description: Published in 1895 and the finest single volume of the Rhymers' Club poets: the lyrics of faith, sin and the English literary past.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Dark Angel', 'Winchester', 'By the Statue of King Charles at Charing Cross', 'The Precept of Silence' and the odes on Oxford and the Catholic martyrs, in which the poet's divided self is the central subject.
historical_context: 1895: the Rhymers' Club, the Catholic revival, and the aestheticised English patriotism of the 1890s.
literary_significance: Poems is the most formally accomplished collection of the English 1890s and contains 'The Dark Angel', the central poem of the Catholic Decadence: its treatment of the divided self made it a permanent text for the modern poetry of contradiction.

title: The Art of Thomas Hardy
description: Published in 1894 and the first book-length study of Hardy's fiction: a critical appreciation by a fellow poet, of Hardy's Wessex, his tragic method and his poetry of place.
plot_or_argument: Johnson examines Hardy's novels in turn, and argues that their power lies in the fusion of a Greek sense of fate with a local English landscape and a modern scepticism.
historical_context: 1894: the Hardy controversy after Tess, the new criticism of the novel, and the Rhymers' Club.
literary_significance: The Art of Thomas Hardy is the founding critical study of Hardy and one of the best books of Victorian criticism: it established Hardy as a tragic novelist rather than a regionalist and shaped all later criticism.

title: Ireland, with Other Poems
description: Published in 1897 and the collection that made Johnson a figure in the Irish revival: the poems on Ireland, its saints and its martyrs, together with the odes and lyrics of his last years.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'Ireland', 'The Dark Angel' (in a revised version), 'Parnell', 'The Abbey of Saint Mary' and the poems of friendship and loneliness; its subject is the Catholic and Celtic past of Ireland and the poet's relation to it.
historical_context: 1897: the Irish Literary Revival, the fall of Parnell, and the English Catholic revival.
literary_significance: Ireland is the finest English-language poetry of the Irish revival by a poet outside Ireland: its poems of the Irish past made Johnson an honorary figure of the movement and influenced Yeats's own early poetry.

title: Post Liminium: Essays and Critical Papers
description: Published posthumously in 1911 and the best collection of Johnson's critical prose: essays on Hardy, Pater, the Celtic literature, the English poets and the Catholic writers.
plot_or_argument: The essays range over Shakespeare and the Elizabethans, the seventeenth-century divines, Pater, Hardy, the Irish poets and the Catholic tradition, and their method is the close reading of a passage in the light of a whole literary and religious tradition.
historical_context: 1890s-1900s: the English Catholic revival, the Irish movement, and the professional criticism of the period.
literary_significance: Post Liminium contains some of the finest critical prose of the 1890s and is the best record of Johnson's learning and his sympathy; it is a key text in the history of English criticism and of the Catholic literary revival.

title: In a Music-Hall and Other Poems
description: Published in 1891 and the most original book of English poetry of its year: the poems of the music hall, the street and the working city that founded the urban poetry of the twentieth century.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'In a Music-Hall', 'The Ballad of a Nun', 'A Ballad of the Two Queens', 'Thirty Bob a Week' and the monologues of the music-hall artiste and the clerk, in which the city is seen as a spectacle and a prison.
historical_context: 1891: the London music hall, the new mass entertainment, and the English reception of the French symbolists.
literary_significance: In a Music-Hall is the founding book of English urban poetry and 'Thirty Bob a Week' is the first great English poem of the white-collar worker: Davidson's music-hall poems changed the subject matter of English verse and influenced Eliot's early poetry directly.

title: 'Thirty Bob a Week'
description: Published in Ballads and Songs in 1894 and the first great English poem about the office worker: the monologue of a clerk living on thirty shillings a week.
plot_or_argument: The clerk describes his life of work, marriage, children and debt, and insists — against the moralists and the socialists — that he 'was built on the rollin' deep' and that his life, if narrow, is his own and not to be pitied.
historical_context: 1890s: the London clerk, the new white-collar class and the monthly salary, and the socialist critique of the 'black-coated proletariat'.
literary_significance: 'Thirty Bob a Week' is the founding English poem of the white-collar worker and one of the most technically original poems of the century: its colloquial voice and its refusal of melodrama made it a model for the modern dramatic monologue, and Eliot named it as an influence.

title: Ballads and Songs
description: Published in 1894 and the best selection of Davidson's shorter poems: the ballads of the city, the dramatic monologues and the lyrics of love and poverty.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'Thirty Bob a Week', 'A Runnable Stag', 'The Crystal Palace', 'The Unknown', 'A Woman and Her Son' and the ballads of Scottish and London life, in which the modern city is rendered with a force unmatched in the poetry of the decade.
historical_context: 1894: the London of the 1890s, the music hall and the street, and the English ballad revival.
literary_significance: Ballads and Songs is the finest single collection of English poetry of the 1890s outside the Rhymers' Club and the central text of the modern ballad: its colloquial energy made it a model for the poetry of Hardy and of the Georgian poets.

title: The Testament of a Vivisector
description: Published in 1901 and the first of Davidson's 'Testaments': a dramatic monologue in which a vivisectionist defends his work against the claims of pity.
plot_or_argument: The vivisector argues that knowledge is the highest good and that the suffering of animals is justified by the advance of science, and the poem sets his argument against the moral imagination of the reader in a way that refuses an easy verdict.
historical_context: 1901: the anti-vivisection movement, the ethics of experimental medicine, and the Nietzschean philosophy of the will.
literary_significance: The Testament of a Vivisector is the most original English poem on the ethics of science and the founding text of the modern poetry of moral argument: its dramatic method of giving the case its strongest voice made it a model for the poetry of debate.

title: 'The Hound of Heaven'
description: Written in 1889 and published in Poems in 1893: the most famous English religious poem of the century, and the record of the soul's flight from the God who pursues it.
plot_or_argument: The speaker describes his flight from the 'Hound of Heaven' through the worlds of nature, art, love and human companionship, and ends with the voice of God: 'All things betray thee, who betrayest Me' and 'thou hast Me, if thou hast Me, at the first'.
meter_and_prosody: Eleven irregular stanzas of long, hovering lines, rhymed irregularly, with internal rhyme and an insistent alliteration.
historical_context: 1889: Thompson's years of destitution in London, the Catholic revival, and the poetry of the seventeenth-century divines.
literary_significance: 'The Hound of Heaven' is the central English religious poem of the nineteenth century after In Memoriam: its image of the pursuing God entered the language, its irregular ode form changed English devotional verse, and it has been recited and anthologised ever since.

title: Poems (Thompson, 1893)
description: Published in 1893 with a preface by Coventry Patmore and the volume that made Thompson famous: the Catholic odes and lyrics of his London years.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Hound of Heaven', 'The Making of Viola', 'Sister Songs', 'A Fallen Yew', 'From the Night of Forebeing' and the poems of childhood and of the Eucharist, and its subject is the relation of human love and divine love.
historical_context: 1893: the Catholic revival, the patronage of the Meynells, and the English reception of the Decadent religious lyric.
literary_significance: Poems is the finest single volume of English Catholic poetry of the century and made Thompson one of the most admired poets of the 1890s: its fusion of baroque imagery and modern suffering created a new kind of devotional poetry.
